profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a tertiary head and neck reconstruction center between the clinical lead for mandibular reconstruction and the evidence-synthesis lead to organize an updated systematic review and meta-analysis on virtual surgical planning (VSP) versus conventional planning in fibula free flap head and neck reconstruction. The update is intended both for submission to a reconstructive surgery journal and to support the hospital's decision about expanding access to VSP workflows. The agenda is to confirm the review scope, decide how studies and outcomes will be classified, assign screening and extraction responsibilities, and set a timeline for protocol, search, screening, and analysis. The expected outcome is a shared plan for launching the review update over the next two weeks, with both participants believing they have aligned on definitions, workflow, and deliverables.

members.name: Dr. Aisling Byrne
members.role: Consultant Maxillofacial Surgeon and Clinical Lead for Microvascular Reconstruction
members.expertise: Fibula free flap reconstruction, mandibular defect planning, VSP implementation in operative practice
members.background: A head and neck reconstructive surgeon who has introduced digital planning tools into selected cases over the past four years and is pushing for broader institutional adoption of VSP pathways.
members.private_state: She wants a timely review that supports clinical adoption of VSP at her center, avoids methodological delays, and reflects real-world reconstructive practice rather than narrow technical distinctions used in evidence-synthesis papers.
hidden_assumptions: If a paper reports 'operative time' in any clinically recognizable way, it is usable because the practical question is whether VSP reduces overall theatre burden.
Digital preoperative planning methods belong in the VSP category even when they use only in-house 3D models or prebent plates without a formal vendor-planned guide set.
A 'pilot' for this review naturally means trying the eligibility and extraction form on a handful of full-text papers, because that is where the clinical ambiguities appear.
Since this is an update of a published review with the same broad question, screening can start immediately and administrative protocol formalities can follow.
Using the prior review's framing should minimize debate, so fine-grained redefinition of old terms is unnecessary unless a problem becomes obvious.

members.name: Dr. Daniel Cho
members.role: Clinical Epidemiologist and Senior Research Fellow in Evidence Synthesis
members.expertise: Systematic reviews, meta-analysis, protocol development, risk-of-bias assessment in surgical literature
members.background: A methodologist embedded in the hospital research institute who supports surgical departments with evidence reviews and is responsible for making the update publishable under current review standards.
members.private_state: He wants the review to be methodologically defensible, reproducible, and compatible with journal and PRISMA expectations, while avoiding preventable heterogeneity and post hoc decisions.
hidden_assumptions: When a team says it will use 'operative time,' it usually means the most comparable operative-duration measure across studies, ideally the reconstructive portion rather than any author-defined total theatre time.

The intervention category 'VSP' should be reserved for formal virtual planning workflows with CAD/CAM guides, cutting jigs, or patient-specific hardware; model-only adjuncts are a different level of intervention.
A 'pilot ten papers' step conventionally refers to a calibration exercise in the screening platform before large-scale title/abstract screening begins.
Using the 'same protocol' means adapting the previous protocol into a current, explicitly documented review plan before screening decisions are made.
If a methodological detail is standard in evidence synthesis, a clinically experienced collaborator will usually be assuming the same standard unless they object.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to extract 'operative time' as a primary outcome.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means any author-reported operative duration that reflects OR efficiency in the case overall, including total incision-to-closure time for combined ablation and reconstruction when that is how surgical papers present it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a comparable operative-duration measure centered on the reconstructive episode, with mixed or broader theatre-time definitions treated cautiously, subgrouped, or effectively deprioritized.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'operative time' sounds fully standard in surgical literature, so each assumes the other is using the obvious meaning; the difference only matters later when papers report slightly different timing windows.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about including 'VSP cases' in the intervention arm.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the intervention arm should include any digitally planned reconstructive workflow, such as vendor-designed guides, in-house 3D printed models, virtual mandibular simulation, or prebent plates prepared from digital planning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the intervention arm should mainly include formal CAD/CAM virtual planning workflows with case-specific guides or custom hardware, while model-only or visualization-only papers are borderline and may belong outside the main intervention set.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have seen the umbrella term VSP used loosely in the literature, so broad agreement on studying 'VSP' masks a meaningful difference in where each thinks the intervention boundary sits.

misalignment_points.topic: What the pilot ten papers step entails
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should 'pilot ten papers' before moving ahead.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means ten full-text articles should be reviewed against the inclusion criteria and extraction sheet to catch clinically messy edge cases early.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means both reviewers should independently screen the first ten citations or abstracts in Covidence to calibrate title/abstract decisions and agreement coding.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Piloting is a routine pre-launch step in reviews, and 'ten papers' sounds concrete enough that neither feels a need to specify whether the pilot is at citation screening, full-text review, or extraction.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'same protocol as the old review' implies
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to use 'the same protocol as the 2018 review' for the update.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presumes the old review question and endpoint structure are already settled, so the team can begin searching and screening immediately while any formal protocol write-up catches up later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presumes that before screening starts, the team will create an updated documented protocol for the new review cycle, including current eligibility language and risk-of-bias handling, even if it is based on the old review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are trying to avoid redesigning the study from scratch, 'same protocol' feels like strong alignment, while the hidden divergence concerns whether protocol work is retrospective shorthand or a prerequisite to starting.

turns.inner_thought: We need this update to move quickly and to be useful for the service case, not disappear into months of methodological tinkering. The 2018 review already set the question broadly enough, so there is no reason to halt while someone rewrites every definition. If we keep the same protocol as the 2018 review and the same headline outcomes, we can start screening straight away and tidy the documentation alongside it. For me, operative time needs to reflect the practical theatre burden surgeons and managers care about, however authors have reported it.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The department really needs an updated review on VSP in fibula free flap reconstruction, both for a journal submission and for our local planning around expanding access. My instinct is that we keep the same protocol as the 2018 review and stick with the core outcomes, so we can get moving without reopening the whole question.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds workable as long as 'same protocol' means I can update the old framework into a current review protocol before screening starts. I can adapt the prior eligibility, build the project in Covidence, rerun the searches, and keep the team aligned with PRISMA expectations. Good that she doesn't want to redesign the review from scratch; we just need a defensible updated plan on paper first.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that's sensible. We can use the same protocol as the 2018 review as the basis, adapt the setup in Covidence, rerun the database searches, and get things moving quickly without reinventing it.

turns.inner_thought: The main reason the unit cares about this is whether VSP changes what happens in theatre and whether it protects flap workflow, so operative time and ischaemic time have to stay front and centre. I don't want the analysis skewed toward narrow technical timings that miss the reality of a combined ablative-reconstructive case if that's how papers report it. If the outcome is recognizably operative time, we should use it.
turns.utterance: For endpoints, I'd keep operative time and ischaemic time as the primary ones again. Those are still the outcomes that matter most when we're asking whether VSP changes workflow in theatre.

turns.inner_thought: Operative time is fine as a primary outcome, but we'll need to be disciplined in extraction so the comparison is as consistent as possible. In surgical reviews, the more comparable measure is usually the reconstructive component, and if papers mix broader timings we'll have to handle that carefully. I don't think she means anything unusual by the term, so we should be aligned there.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Operative time should work well as long as we're consistent in how we extract it, and ischaemic time is usually reported clearly enough to sit alongside it. We can standardize as much as the literature allows.

turns.inner_thought: I do not want the intervention arm artificially narrowed to only the most commercialized workflows. In real mandibular reconstruction, surgeons use a spectrum of digital planning approaches, and if we exclude in-house planning, models, or prebent plate workflows, the review won't reflect practice or help our institution. All of that belongs under VSP cases for this question.
turns.utterance: On the intervention side, I think we should make sure we're capturing VSP cases broadly, because in the papers and in practice people use a mix of approaches under that heading. I wouldn't want us to miss relevant studies simply because the workflow isn't described in exactly the same way every time.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine for now. We can keep VSP cases as the umbrella label while I mentally separate the clearer CAD/CAM-type interventions from the more borderline adjuncts. If we tag the straightforward ones first, we can preserve a cleaner main analysis and decide later how to handle the less formal workflows without arguing about it now.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Let's keep VSP cases as the intervention arm and, as we go, tag the more straightforward ones first so we have a clear map of what's in the evidence base.

turns.inner_thought: Before the registrar gets involved, I want to test the inclusion criteria and extraction sheet on actual full-text studies, because that's where the fibula-specific nuances and messy clinical judgment calls show up. A pilot ten papers this week should tell us whether the old framing still works and whether the data fields capture what matters.
turns.utterance: Why don't we pilot ten papers this week? That should let us see where the fibula-specific edge cases sit before I pull the registrar into the review work.

turns.inner_thought: Good, a pilot ten papers step is exactly what we need for calibration before opening the floodgates on title and abstract screening. I'll check agreement in Covidence once we've both done the first ten records, then we can move into the main screening phase with fewer preventable discrepancies. Nice that she's on board with a standard pilot.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's a good idea. Once we've pilot ten papers, I'll look at the agreement in Covidence and then we can open the main screening phase.

turns.inner_thought: There's no need to wait for administrative polishing to begin identifying likely papers. Since we're using the same protocol as the 2018 review, I can start right away with the journals most likely to contain the clinically relevant fibula series. That should speed things up and keep the review grounded in the reconstructive literature rather than purely database mechanics.
turns.utterance: In the meantime, I can start pulling likely studies from the recent microsurgery and maxillofacial journals straight away, since we're basically using the same protocol as before. That should help us build momentum.

turns.inner_thought: I'll need to get the updated review package in place properly: protocol adaptation, search rerun, Covidence project, and the pilot workflow, then screening can begin next week once those pieces are set.
